newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Asterix quits retirement to fight again for Gaul.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asterix quits retirement to fight again for Gaul.

text.p: Asterix the Gaul leaves cartoon retirement this month to take another swig of magic potion, beat up Romans and travel abroad with his chunky friend Obelix. And comic strip centurions are not the only ones trembling.

"I'm very scared," said author and illustrator Albert Uderzo of the October 10 relaunch, despite a winning formula that has brought worldwide sales of 280 million books since tiny Asterix became a Gallic freedom-fighter in 1959.

"The older I get, the more success I achieve, the more frightened I am," the grey-haired Uderzo said of his first Asterix title since "Asterix and the Secret Weapon" in 1991 and the 30th in the series.

Uderzo, 69, said he was gambling with a giant initial print run of eight million books in 15 languages -- a record for Asterix and one of the biggest in publishing history. Stacked up, they would create a pile about 80 km (50 miles) high.
"We can't afford any mistakes," he said. "The reader also gets used to success. He must always feel disturbed, surprised or shocked. The day he no longer feels this, he'll leave you."

Uderzo has even gagged himself about the title of the new book, about wily Asterix and friends in the only village holding out against the Roman occupation of Gaul in 50 B.C., helped by a strength-giving magic potion brewed by village druid Getafix.

"It will be a trip. (Asterix and Obelix) will leave Gaul, to a destination sadly unknown, where they arrive safely and they also return. And it ends happily," he told Reuters in his Paris office stuffed with spin-offs, including Obelix recipe books.
He said the trip would be to a country the pair had not yet visited -- ruling out nations including Spain, Britain, Italy, Belgium and the United States.

He denied one media report that Obelix, endearingly daft and hugely strong, would be the first person to die in the cartoons -- Romans only ever get groggy despite repeated bashings. "I'm not so mad as to kill off my characters," he said.

He refused comment on media suggestions the two would travel to China from their village on the northwest coast of France, saying they were mere rumours. And he reassured fans that "all the traditions that people link with Asterix will be there."
So the book will be stuffed with puns, Obelix will carry huge rocks as a menhir-delivery-man, gorge himself on roasted boar, the pair will assault Romans and a pirate boat will sink.
The new book is the sixth Uderzo has written alone since the 1977 death of partner Rene Goscinny, who used to write the stories with Uderzo supplying the drawings.

Uderzo said he felt obliged to produce a new book and felt guilty about the long gap since the last. He also regrets announcing in 1994 that he was retiring and that Asterix had hung up his sword for good.
"I had a moment of weakness, of fatigue. I had legal problems with my former publisher. I was disappointed by a court ruling and I said to myself: "I am stopping'.
"But it would be stupid to stop."
In 1994, Uderzo and Goscinny's family lost a claim for compensation from former publisher Dargaud for copyright payments they were claiming from Dargaud's foreign subsidiaries.
Asterix, now published by "Editions Albert-Rene", has proved a gold mine with its David and Goliath theme of plucky Gallic villagers defying the might of Julius Caesar's empire.

Yet Uderzo says he is at a loss to explain Asterix's success. Asterix's combined sales of 280 million are about 100 million more than the total sales of Herge's Tintin books, Asterix's closest comic rival in Europe.
"We're public jesters. We want to make people smile. With the times we have today, I think it's a necessary medicine," he said.

The books have inspired the Parc Asterix theme park north of Paris, which opened in 1989 and is a rival to the Disneyland Paris park east of the capital. Uderzo concedes his books have never had big success in the U.S., the land of Mickey Mouse.

And there are plans to open an Asterix site on the Internet computer system late this month and perhaps make a film with bulky French actor Gerard Depardieu cast as Obelix and Daniel Auteuil as Asterix.

The cartoons have sometimes been accused of misogyny or racism. Uderzo said he told feminists: "Look at the way I depict the men physically. If I treated the women like I treat the men, they you'd have reason to call me a misogynist".
He also rebuffed suggestions the books were racist because Romans were portrayed as daft and cruel and always ended up as battered losers. Uderzo said the books sold well in Italy.
He said he planned to continue writing Asterix books but would not let ghost writers take over when he died. "It will end. After the death of the two authors, the strip cartoon is finished."
